sections.b: The Shema begins in Deuteronomy 6:4–9: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). The words are to be kept on the heart, taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on the hand and between the eyes, and written on doorposts. Deuteronomy 11:13–21 repeats the commands with the promise of rain and the warning of drought; the rabbis joined it and Numbers 15:37–41 to form the prayer said every morning and evening. The six Hebrew words of 6:4 can be read as "the LORD is our God, the LORD alone," "the LORD our God is one LORD," or as on this site, and every reading joins loyalty with unity. The command to love borrows the language of treaties, where love meant loyal service to a king.

Asked which command is first, Jesus quotes the Shema with its opening line and adds "with all your mind," then joins it with "love your neighbor" (Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 22:34–40; Luke 10:25–28). Paul's "one God, the Father ... one Lord, Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 8:6) reworks the Shema's words. Christians from the 4th century on argued that the word echad, "one," allows a unity with distinctions, a reading Jewish teachers reject.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 22:34–40; Luke 10:25–28; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; James 2:19

common: The Shema is the basic confession of Jewish faith, recited twice daily and at the moment of death.
uncommon: Some scholars think "the LORD is one" first meant one LORD as against local forms such as "YHWH of Samaria" and "YHWH of Teman" known from Kuntillet Ajrud.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 4 states Israel's faith in one God more sharply than any earlier book: "the LORD is God. Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35), and "the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39). The proof is history: no people has heard a god speak out of fire and lived, or been taken out of another nation by signs and wonders (4:32–34). Yet the same book calls the LORD "the God of gods and the Lord of lords" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and says the sky's lights were given as a share to the nations (4:19). Nathan MacDonald argues that Deuteronomy calls for exclusive loyalty more than it defines God philosophically; Mark Smith sees a move from an older council of gods to strict monotheism in the exile; traditional readers take the statements of chapter 4 as final.

common: Deuteronomy 4:35 and 4:39 are among the Old Testament's clearest statements that only one God exists.
uncommon: Some scholars read "There is no other" as a claim about Israel's loyalty, not yet a denial that other gods exist.

sections.b: Deuteronomy's asides list peoples remembered as huge: the Emim in Moab, the Zamzummim in Ammon and the Anakim, all counted among the Rephaim (Deuteronomy 2:10–11; Deuteronomy 2:20–21). God drove them out for Lot's and Esau's descendants just as he would for Israel, so the giants that frightened Israel's scouts (1:28) were no obstacle to God. Og king of Bashan alone "was left of the last of the Rephaim," and his iron bed was nine cubits long (3:11). In 9:2 the people quote a proverb: "Who can stand up to the sons of Anak?" Readers have taken these as memories of tall peoples, legends of a heroic past, or, in some ancient Jewish writings, as the offspring of the Nephilim of Genesis 6.

common: Og's bed has long been read as proof that the Rephaim were literal giants.
uncommon: Some scholars connect Og's bed with the stone dolmens of the Golan and Gilead, ancient tombs of huge slabs.

sections.b: Martin Noth (1943) argued that Deuteronomy 1–3, or 1–4, was written not as Moses' review but as the opening of a long history that runs through Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings. Its retelling of Horeb, Kadesh and the eastern victories leads straight into Joshua, which begins where Deuteronomy 3:28 and 31:7–8 leave off, with the charge to Joshua to be brave and strong. The language of these chapters, the warnings of exile in chapter 4, and the themes of obedience and the land run through the whole history. Frank Moore Cross saw two editions, one under King Josiah and one in the exile. Traditional readers see the same links as signs that later books were written in the light of Deuteronomy, not that Deuteronomy was written for them.

common: Most critical scholars hold that Deuteronomy shaped the books from Joshua to Kings.
uncommon: Some recent scholars doubt there was ever a single Deuteronomistic History, and see separate books edited in different ways.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 11:26–28 sums up the opening sermons as a choice: "Look: I am putting a blessing and a curse in front of you today" (Deuteronomy 11:26), the blessing if Israel keeps God's commands and the curse if it turns to other gods. The choice is to be enacted on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal near Shechem (11:29–30). Earlier, 7:12–16 lists blessings on children, herds, crops and health for a loyal people, and 11:13–17 ties rain itself to loyalty. Like the blessings and curses of ancient treaties, these are the sanctions of the covenant, spelled out fully in chapters 27–28.

common: The blessings and curses are often read as a promise that faithfulness always brings prosperity.
uncommon: Some readers stress that the blessings are given to the people as a whole, not promised to each individual.

sections.b: Deuteronomy calls itself torah, "law" or "instruction" (Deuteronomy 1:5; Deuteronomy 4:44), and Moses begins "to make this law clear" on the plains of Moab. Its law is meant to be understood and loved: Israel is not to add to it or take away from it (4:2), and it will be their wisdom in the eyes of the nations, who will say, "This great nation is surely a wise and understanding people!" (Deuteronomy 4:6). The law comes in layers: the Ten Words spoken by God to all (5:6–21), then "the whole command, the rules and the rulings" given through Moses (5:31), which chapters 12–26 set out. When a child asks what the laws mean, the answer is the story of the exodus (6:20–25).

common: The name "Deuteronomy" means "second law," though the book presents itself as an explanation of the one law.
uncommon: Bernard Levinson argues that Deuteronomy rewrote older laws boldly while presenting itself as their faithful repetition.

sections.h: The covenant at Horeb, renewed in Moab
sections.b: Deuteronomy 1–11 retells the covenant made at Horeb and applies it to a new generation: "The LORD did not make this covenant with our ancestors. He made it with us, we who are here today, all of us alive" (Deuteronomy 5:3). The Ten Words are its terms, written on two tablets (4:13; 5:22). The covenant is broken with the golden calf, and renewed with new tablets kept in the ark (9:7–10:5). God keeps "his covenant and his loyal love for a thousand generations" (Deuteronomy 7:9). Scholars compare the book's shape to ancient treaties, with their history, terms, witnesses and blessings and curses; chapter 4 even calls heaven and earth as witnesses (4:26).

common: Deuteronomy is shaped like a treaty between a great king and his people.
uncommon: Some scholars read the covenant language as borrowed directly from Assyrian loyalty oaths of the 7th century BC.

sections.b: Deuteronomy is Moses' last words. In chapters 1–11 he looks back on forty years: the burden of leading a people he could not carry alone (1:9–12), the failure at Kadesh, his forty days on his face before God after the golden calf (9:18; 9:25–29), and his own exclusion from the land. Three times he says God was angry with him "because of you" (1:37; 3:26; 4:21), and his prayer to cross over is refused: "That is enough from you!" (3:26). He may only see the land from Pisgah and must give Joshua his charge (3:27–28). The rabbis counted his prayer as the model of asking with praise first.

common: Moses was barred from the land because he struck the rock at Meribah.
uncommon: Deuteronomy 1:37 and 3:26 suggest Moses was barred because he shared the guilt of the people at Kadesh.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 5:6–21 gives the second form of the Ten Words, and Deuteronomy 4:13 and 10:4 give the name "the Ten Words." The two forms differ in about twenty details. The Sabbath command says "Keep" for Exodus's "Remember" and grounds the day in the memory of slavery: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15), not in creation. The command to honor parents adds "so that it will go well with you." The last command puts the neighbor's wife first, adds "his field," and uses two verbs, "crave" and "long for" (5:21). After the Ten Words, God "added nothing more" (5:22) and wrote them on two tablets, which were later replaced and kept in the ark (10:1–5).

common: The Sabbath in Deuteronomy looks back to the exodus, the Sabbath in Exodus to creation.
uncommon: The rabbis taught that God spoke "keep" and "remember" in one word, at the same moment.

sections.b: Deuteronomy gives the Bible's clearest teaching on why God chose Israel. It was not size: "you were the fewest of all the peoples" (Deuteronomy 7:7). It was not righteousness: "it is not because you are righteous... You are a stiff-necked people" (9:6). It was love and promise: "It was because the LORD loved you, and because he kept the oath he swore to your ancestors" (Deuteronomy 7:8). Israel is God's "own private treasure" (7:6), and the God to whom "the sky belongs... even the highest heavens" set his heart on its ancestors (10:14–15). Election brings duty: holiness, loyalty and love for the foreigner (10:19).

common: God chose Israel out of love, not because of any merit of its own.
uncommon: Jon Levenson reads election as the love of a father for a beloved son, which brings suffering as well as privilege.

sections.b: Deuteronomy commands Israel to put the nations of Canaan "under the ban" (cherem), devoting them to destruction (Deuteronomy 7:1–2), and reports that Israel did this to the towns of Sihon and Og (2:34; 3:6). The same chapters tell Israel to leave Edom, Moab and Ammon in peace, because God gave them their lands (2:4–19). The reason given for the ban is worship: the nations "will turn your sons away from following me" (Deuteronomy 7:4). Readers explain the command as a unique judgment for the nations' sin (9:4–5), as ancient war rhetoric (since 7:3 forbids marrying the same peoples and 7:22 says they will be cleared "bit by bit"), as a late ideal against idolatry, or as a view later Scripture moves beyond.

common: The ban commanded the total destruction of the Canaanite peoples.
uncommon: Some scholars read the ban as hyperbole, since the same text assumes the peoples will remain to be married or slowly driven out.

sections.h: Sihon and Og in Moses' memory
sections.b: Deuteronomy tells the victories over Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan from Moses' point of view. Sihon is offered peace and refuses, because God "made his spirit hard and his heart stubborn" (Deuteronomy 2:30). Og comes out to fight at Edrei and is defeated, and sixty walled towns are taken (3:1–7). Og alone "was left of the last of the Rephaim," with a famous iron bed (3:11). The two kings become a standard memory of God's power, recalled in 4:46–47 and later by Rahab, the Psalms and Nehemiah.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 2:24–37; Deuteronomy 3:1–11; Deuteronomy 4:46–47; Joshua 2:10; Psalm 135:10–12; Psalm 136:17–22

common: Sihon and Og were the first kings defeated in the conquest.

sections.b: In Deuteronomy 9:7–10:11 Moses retells the golden calf as proof that Israel did not earn the land. He was on the mountain forty days receiving the tablets "written by the finger of God" (9:10) when God told him the people had made an idol. He came down, smashed the tablets before their eyes, burned the calf, ground it to dust and threw it into the stream (9:15–21). He lay before God forty days and nights, praying for the people and for Aaron, whom God was angry enough to destroy (9:18–20; 9:25–29). Compared with Exodus 32–34, Deuteronomy shifts the long prayer after the descent, leaves out the Levites' slaughter, and stresses Moses' intercession.

common: Aaron made the calf, and Moses' prayer saved the people from destruction.
uncommon: Only Deuteronomy says that God was angry enough to destroy Aaron (9:20).

sections.b: Moses' prayer in Deuteronomy 9:25–29 is one of the Bible's great intercessions. God says, "Let go of me, so I can destroy them" (Deuteronomy 9:14), and Moses does not let go. He lies on his face forty days and nights (9:18; 9:25), and prays without appealing to Israel's merit: they are God's people and inheritance, redeemed by his power; God should remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and not look at Israel's stubbornness; and Egypt would say the LORD could not bring them in (9:26–29). God listens (10:10). But when Moses prays for himself, to cross the Jordan, the answer is no (3:23–26).

claude.title: Claude's note: a prayer that wins for others and loses for himself
claude.body: My own observation: Deuteronomy sets Moses' two prayers side by side in the same sermon. The prayer for the people is granted (10:10); the prayer for himself is refused (3:26). The book seems to want both remembered: the mediator who saves others does not save his own place in the land.

sections.b: Deuteronomy grounds the ban on images in what Israel saw, or did not see, at Horeb: "You saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the fire" (Deuteronomy 4:15). Therefore no image of man or woman, animal, bird, creeping thing or fish may be made, and the sun, moon and stars must not be worshiped (4:16–19). The list runs back through the creation order of Genesis 1. Israel must burn the idols of Canaan and not crave their silver and gold, since they are abhorrent to God (7:5; 7:25–26). The golden calf (9:12–21) shows how quickly the people broke this command.

Deuteronomy's form of the Sabbath command (Deuteronomy 5:12–15) says "Keep" rather than "Remember" and adds a social purpose: "Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do" (Deuteronomy 5:14). Its reason is the exodus: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15). Where Exodus 20:11 grounds the day in creation, Deuteronomy grounds it in liberation. Jewish worship joins both reasons: the Friday-night blessing over wine calls the Sabbath a memorial of creation and of the exodus, and a scroll from Qumran (4QDeut-n) adds the creation reason to Deuteronomy's text.

common: Deuteronomy links the Sabbath to the exodus, Exodus to creation.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 10:16 commands: "So circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer" (Deuteronomy 10:16). A heart with a "foreskin" is one closed to God, as an uncircumcised ear cannot hear (Jeremiah 6:10). The command comes in a passage on love for the foreigner and the God who shows no favoritism (10:17–19). Later in the book God promises to do it himself (see 30:6). Jeremiah takes up the image (Jeremiah 4:4), and Paul writes that true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29).

common: Circumcision of the heart means a heart open and obedient to God.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 1–11 describes the land Israel is about to enter as "a good land. It is a land of streams of water" (Deuteronomy 8:7), of wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olive oil and honey, with iron and copper in its hills (8:7–9). Unlike Egypt, watered by the Nile, it "drinks water from the rain of the sky" and God's eyes are on it all year (Deuteronomy 11:11–12). It comes with cities, houses, wells and vineyards Israel did not make (6:10–11). The land is a gift sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (1:8), and its borders run from the wilderness to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the western sea (11:24). Holding it depends on loyalty (4:25–27; 11:17).

common: The land of Israel is described as "a land flowing with milk and honey."

sections.b: In Deuteronomy the forty years are remembered both as punishment and as training. God led Israel "to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2); he fed them with manna and trained them "the way a man trains his son" (8:5). Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell (8:4). The wilderness was "huge and fearsome," full of burning snakes and scorpions (1:19; 8:15), yet "You have not lacked a thing" (2:7). By the brook Zered the generation of fighting men had died, as God swore (2:14–16).

sections.b: Deuteronomy 1:19–46 retells the failure at Kadesh-barnea. The people propose sending scouts (1:22), who bring back fruit and a good report, but the people refuse to go up, saying God hated them and brought them out to destroy them (1:26–28). God swears that none of that generation will see the land but Caleb and Joshua (1:34–39). The people then attack without God and are routed as far as Hormah (1:41–44). "So you stayed in Kadesh many days" (Deuteronomy 1:46). In Numbers 13:1–2 the scouts are sent at God's command; Deuteronomy puts the idea with the people.

common: Kadesh is where Israel refused to enter the land and was condemned to forty years of wandering.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 10:17–19 grounds care for the foreigner in God's own character. The God of gods "does not play favorites... He loves the foreigner and gives him food and clothing. So you are to love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:17–19). The foreigner (ger), a resident outsider without land or family protection, also rests on the Sabbath (5:14). The same chapters that command the ban on the Canaanites protect Edom, Moab and Ammon in their own lands (2:4–19), and call Israel to love the outsider who lives among them.

common: Deuteronomy commands Israel not only to tolerate but to love the foreigner.

sections.b: In Deuteronomy 10:1–5 God tells Moses to make "a wooden ark" along with the new tablets, and Moses makes it of acacia wood and puts the tablets in it, "and they are still there" (10:5). Deuteronomy describes the ark simply, as a container for the covenant, without the gold covering and cherubim of Exodus 25 and 37. The tribe of Levi is chosen to carry it (10:8). The rabbis said that both the broken and the whole tablets were kept inside (Bavli Berakhot 8b).

Deuteronomy 10:8–9 records that God "set apart the tribe of Levi" to carry the ark of the covenant, to stand before the LORD to serve him, and to bless in his name. Levi has no portion or inheritance with its brothers; "the LORD is his inheritance." Deuteronomy usually speaks of "the Levite priests" as one group, while Numbers and Leviticus distinguish Aaron's sons from the other Levites, a difference much discussed by scholars.

sections.h: Three towns east of the Jordan
sections.b: Moses sets apart three towns east of the Jordan for anyone who kills a neighbor without intent and without old hatred: Bezer for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh (Deuteronomy 4:41–43). Chapter 19 gives the full law for the towns west of the Jordan (see 19:1–13).

On the way north Israel is told to pass by "your brothers, the descendants of Esau," not to start a fight, and to pay for food and water, because God has given Mount Seir to Esau (Deuteronomy 2:4–6). An aside says the Horites once lived in Seir and Esau's descendants drove them out (2:12; 2:22). In Numbers 20:14–21 Edom refuses passage; Deuteronomy's friendlier account is often noted by scholars.

Deuteronomy 2:9–19 protects Moab and Ammon as the descendants of Lot, to whom God gave Ar and the land of the Ammonites. The Emim had lived in Moab, and the Zamzummim in Ammon (2:10–11; 2:20–21). Israel is not to harass them. The whole book is spoken "in the land of Moab" (1:5), on the plains across from Jericho.

At Horeb the people "were hearing the sound of words, but... seeing no form" (Deuteronomy 4:12). Deuteronomy builds its ban on images on this. Yet the people say, "Today we have seen that God can speak with a human being and the person still lives" (Deuteronomy 5:24), and Moses asks, "Has any people heard the voice of a god speaking out of fire, as you have heard it, and lived?" (Deuteronomy 4:33). Deuteronomy stresses hearing over seeing.

Deuteronomy 8:3 gives the meaning of the manna: God let Israel go hungry and fed them with food unknown to them or their ancestors "to teach you that people do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth" (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus answers the devil with this verse (Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4). Deuteronomy 8:16 calls the manna a test meant to do Israel good in the end.

common: "Man shall not live by bread alone" (Deuteronomy 8:3, KJV) is one of the Bible's most quoted sayings.

sections.b: In Deuteronomy 1–11 Joshua appears as one of the two of the Kadesh generation who will enter the land (1:38), and as Moses' successor: Moses is told to give him his orders and make him brave and strong, "because he will cross over at the head of this people" (Deuteronomy 3:28). Moses encourages him with the victories over Sihon and Og (3:21–22).

In Moses' retelling of Kadesh, Caleb son of Jephunneh is the one exception to God's oath: "Only Caleb son of Jephunneh will see it... because he followed the LORD fully" (Deuteronomy 1:36). Joshua 14:6–14 tells how Caleb claimed Hebron on the strength of this promise.
